mcqs.question: Why does `cd ..` work without the shell parsing or storing any string path arithmetic?
options: The kernel maintains a global map of every directory's full path
Every directory contains a `..` entry that already points to the parent's inode number, so `cd ..` is just an ordinary lookup
The shell recomputes the entire path from root each time
`..` is a special kernel syscall unrelated to directory entries
mcqs.explanation: Every directory has `.` and `..` entries by convention, pointing to its own and its parent's inode. Moving up is just following that existing entry — no path-string computation or global path map needed.

mcqs.question: Two processes have different current working directories and both run `open("../notes.txt")`. Why might they open different files?
options: Relative paths resolve starting from each process's own current working directory, so the same relative string can point to different files
This is a bug — relative paths must always resolve identically for all processes
../ always refers to the file system root regardless of context
Only one process can use a relative path at a time; the other gets an error
mcqs.explanation: Relative path resolution is anchored at the calling process's cwd, tracked per-process by the kernel. Different cwds mean the identical string `../notes.txt` legitimately resolves to different files — this isn't an error condition.

mcqs.question: Before running `mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/backup`, `/mnt/backup` was an empty directory with a few bytes of leftover files on the root file system. After mounting, what happens to those original files?
options: They are deleted to make room for the new file system
They are merged with sdb1's content, appearing side by side
They become temporarily invisible — hidden underneath the mount — and reappear if sdb1 is unmounted
The mount fails because the directory wasn't empty
mcqs.explanation: Mounting doesn't touch the underlying directory's original content — it's shadowed, not deleted or merged. Unmounting sdb1 reveals the original root-filesystem content again, which is a common source of confusion ("my files disappeared") when someone mounts over a non-empty directory.

mcqs.question: Why can't you create a hard link between a file on `/` and a file on a separately mounted partition at `/mnt/data`, even though both paths look like they're under the same tree?
options: Hard links are disabled by default for security reasons
The mount point directory itself is read-only
Inode numbers are only meaningful within one file system; the two mounted file systems have entirely separate, incomparable inode tables
Only symbolic links are allowed anywhere in a Unix tree
mcqs.explanation: A hard link is fundamentally a second directory entry pointing at the same inode number, but inode numbers are scoped per file system. Across a mount boundary there's no shared inode table to reference, so the kernel rejects cross-filesystem hard links.

mcqs.question: `open("/data/reports/q3.csv")` fails with a permission error, but the file owner insists q3.csv has correct read permissions. What should you check first?
options: Whether q3.csv itself is corrupted
Whether every directory in the path — /data and /data/reports — grants execute permission to traverse through it
Whether the disk has enough free space
Whether the file's extension is recognized by the kernel
mcqs.explanation: Path resolution fails at the first broken link, and traversing a directory requires execute permission on that directory, not on the final file. A missing execute bit on an intermediate directory produces exactly this confusing symptom — correct permissions on the target file, but resolution still fails.
